title: Building a robust body
summary: Where tennis players usually run into problems, and how your programme gets each of those areas ready for the load of tennis.

p: Tennis means thousands of serves, shots, stops and pushes every season. Robustness means slowly and steadily getting the parts of your body that take most of that load ready for it.
Muscles and tendons get stronger when they're loaded step by step, on a regular basis. That's why robustness work gets a bit harder week by week, just like your weights.
list: Strength days: calves, rotator cuff, groin, hamstrings, forearm and wrist, and trunk.
Every warm-up: foot and ankle, balance on one leg and mobility.
Home robustness sessions, if Amir adds them: shins and calves, groin, shoulder, trunk, and mobility for the hips, upper back and hamstrings.
Where each piece goes depends on you. Your programme is built around your body and your tennis week.
sections.callout: Robustness means getting your body ready for the load of tennis. No programme can promise you won't get injured, and yours doesn't either.

sections.h: Where do tennis players get problems most?
p: Research on recreational, college and professional players shows where problems happen most. In the legs, sudden injuries like a rolled ankle are more common. In the arm, it's problems that build slowly from lots of repetition, like pain on the outside of the elbow in recreational players and shoulder pain in high level players.
list: Shoulder
Elbow, forearm and wrist
Trunk: lower back, abs and sides
Hip and groin
Thigh and hamstrings
Knee
Ankle and foot
sections.callout: These studies only show where problems happen most. None of them show that training these areas prevents those problems. Strength training does lower injuries in sport in general: a 2014 review of 25 trials found it cut them to less than a third. But the one tennis trial we found was an unsupervised 12 week online programme, and its injury rate was no lower than the control group's. That tested only that one programme. It doesn't prove that supervised work fails.

p: The rotator cuff is a group of small muscles around the shoulder joint that keep the top of your arm in its socket. In serves and overheads, these muscles control the arm and help slow it down after the shot.
Your programme makes the back of the shoulder and the muscles around the shoulder blade stronger, and it doesn't let pushing get ahead of pulling.
list: Turning the arm out: Band External Rotation, Side Lying Dumbbell External Rotation and Cable External Rotation.
Incline Y Raise for the lower shoulder blade muscles.
Band Pull-Apart in your warm-ups.
Over a week, you'll usually do more pulling sets (rows and chin-ups) than pushing sets. That's the course's own rule of thumb, not a study result.
sections.callout: Shoulder exercises are light but their job matters. Slow and controlled, not heavy and swinging.

p: Your forearm holds the racket and keeps the wrist steady on every shot. The tendons on the back of the forearm, which attach to the outside of the elbow, take a lot of load in tennis.
Your forearm work usually changes from cycle to cycle.
list: Single-Arm Eccentric Wrist Extension: you lower the wrist slowly.
Single-Arm Wrist Extension: you lift the wrist up and lower it down.
Pulls and carries work the hand and forearm too: Chin-Up, rows, Suitcase Carry, Overhead Carry and Front-Rack Carry.
sections.callout: These exercises are there to get your arm ready for the load of tennis, not to make your serve faster. The research on lowering a weight slowly is in people who already have tennis elbow. Nobody has shown that it stops it starting.

p: Tennis shots start from the legs and travel through the trunk to the arm. Your trunk has to make rotation and also stop extra rotation.

The groin takes a lot of load in side to side movement, reaching wide for balls and braking at the side of the court. The Copenhagen Plank is from the same family of exercises that cut groin problems in a football trial. That result isn't from tennis, and linking it to tennis is the course's own reasoning.
list: Trunk: Side Plank, Suitcase Carry, Half-Kneeling Pallof Press, Cable Wood Chop and Dead Bug. Harder versions of the same moves come later.
Groin: Copenhagen Plank, a side plank where the inside of your top leg holds your body up.
Adductor Squeeze, for groin strength without moving.
Hips: Lateral Lunge and World's Greatest Stretch in the warm-up, and 90/90 Hip Switch and Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch for mobility.
sections.callout: Tap any of these on your card to see its video and cues. If one is too hard or too easy, tell Amir and he'll give you an easier or harder version.

p: Your hamstrings work hard in sprinting and braking. They control the leg when it's out in front and straight. The research showing fewer hamstring injuries with the Nordic Hamstring Curl was in athletes in other sports, not tennis.
Your knees take load in every landing, stop and change of direction. Your programme builds that load up slowly, with leg strength and with practice at landing and braking.
list: Hamstrings: Stability Ball Leg Curl early on, then Nordic Hamstring Curl once you're ready. Dumbbell Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift and Dumbbell B-Stance Romanian Deadlift strengthen the hamstrings and hips too.
Leg strength: your main lift (like a Trap Bar Deadlift or Barbell Back Squat) and single leg moves like Dumbbell Split Squat and Dumbbell Bulgarian Split Squat.
Landing: you practise landing and holding still before harder jumps, for example with Snap Down and Box Drop.
Braking: the approach speed and the sharpness of the angle go up slowly, and the number of hard stops each week has a limit.
sections.warn: Growing player: take pain right below the kneecap or at the back of the heel seriously, even if it's mild. Tell Amir and read the lesson on growth spurts for players and parents.
sections.callout: More on landing and braking is in the lessons on jumping and landing, and on speed, braking and changing direction.

p: Every step, split step and stop starts at the ankle and foot. Your calf and Achilles tendon work like a spring, taking the force of landing and giving it back.
list: In your warm-ups: Short Foot (barefoot), Ankle Dorsiflexion Rocks and Single-Leg Balance.
Straight leg calf work: Standing Dumbbell Single Leg Calf Raise, or Standing Machine Calf Raise.
Bent knee calf and shin work: Seated Dumbbell Calf Raise and Tibialis Raise.
Short Pogo Jumps in your warm-up get the ankle ready for quick contacts with the ground.
sections.callout: Research shows the foot is one of the common problem areas in women's tennis. That's why foot work is in your warm-ups. That choice is the course's own reasoning. No trial has shown that foot work lowers those problems.

p: Mobility means you can move through your full range with control. For example the hips for open stance shots, or the upper back for the rotation of the serve. In your programme mobility is part of getting ready, not separate stretching sessions.

A home robustness and mobility session is about 30 to 40 minutes, with a band, light dumbbells or water bottles, a chair and a mat. It's written at RPE 7 or below, so it's fine if you're under 16 too. That ceiling is the course's own rule of thumb, not a study result.
list: In your warm-ups: World's Greatest Stretch, Leg Swings, Lateral Lunge and Open Book.
At home: 90/90 Hip Switch, Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch, Quadruped Thoracic Rotation and Supine Strap Hamstring Stretch.
On heavy tennis weeks this is the kind of work that still fits.
It's light and fits on any day, even a tennis day.
sections.warn: Robustness work isn't treatment. Pain that gets worse with training, wakes you at night or comes with swelling? Don't train that area. Tell Amir and read the lesson on pain, soreness and warning signs.
sections.callout: A home session like this is for when your body feels stiff, you have small aches or your tennis week is heavy. Ask Amir if you think you need one.
